fields.h1: Build Incident Response Automation Around Your Playbooks
fields.hero_description: Build incident response automation that groups alerts, pages on-call, and waits for approval before any containment step.
fields.features_heading: What Runs the Moment an Alert Fires
fields.features_subheading: Routine checks and paging run on their own, and every step that changes a system waits for a person to approve it.
fields.feature_1:
Related alerts grouped into one incident

Groups alerts from your monitoring and security tools by host, user, or service. The on-call engineer opens one incident with every related alert attached, not forty pages.
fields.feature_2:
Severity set by rules you write

Assigns severity from rules your team writes, such as Sev 1 for a customer-facing outage and Sev 3 for one failed backup. Each level carries its own paging path and response target.
fields.feature_3:
Pages that escalate on a timer

Pages the primary on-call engineer in Slack and by email, then starts a timer. If nobody acknowledges inside your window, the page moves to the secondary, then the team lead.
fields.feature_4:
Indicators checked before anyone looks

Looks up each indicator as the alert arrives, including the sender domain's age and the link's reputation in your threat feed. The analyst opens the case with answers ready.
fields.feature_5:
Containment held for a person's yes

Prepares the containment step, such as revoking sessions or purging an email, and sends it to the analyst with an approve button. Nothing on a live system changes before then.
fields.feature_6:
Playbooks you keep as code

Exports your rules and integrations as readable code to your GitHub repository on paid plans. Every incident, with its timeline and approvals, sits in a database your team owns.

fields.usecase_heading: Playbooks Security and IT Teams Run First
fields.tab_content_1:
Fourteen phishing reports collapse into one incident

Employees forward suspicious mail to a report address. When 14 reports of the same fake invoice land within 20 minutes, the app files them under INC-2291 and checks the sender domain against your threat feed. Dana Okafor on the security desk gets one request: purge the message from every inbox.
fields.tab_content_2:
Sessions stay open until an analyst approves

Your identity provider flags a sign-in for Ben Carter from Lisbon, 38 minutes after his last one from Denver. The app pulls his 10 most recent sign-ins. Leah Novak, the analyst on call, gets a direct message with one button: revoke his sessions and require a new password. Nothing changes until she clicks.
fields.tab_content_3:
No acknowledgment in 5 minutes pages the backup

Failed checkouts climb past 40 a minute and stay there for 3 minutes. The app opens INC-0412 as Sev 1, starts a Slack channel for it, and pages Chris Doyle, the primary on-call engineer. Five minutes pass without an acknowledgment, and the page moves to Aisha Grant, the secondary, with the error graph attached.
fields.tab_content_4:
The review opens with its timeline already built

INC-0412 closes at 3:20 PM, and the app builds the review from alert events and channel messages. The timeline shows detection at 2:02 PM, acknowledgment at 2:09 PM, and mitigation at 2:41 PM, 39 minutes after the first alert. Three action items go to named owners, each open on the review board until it is done.

fields.howto_description: Seven steps to set up incident response automation that pages the right person and holds risky actions for an analyst's approval.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Pick the incident you handle most
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Write the playbook in plain steps
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Connect the tools that raise alerts
fields.howto_step_1_des: Pull the last 90 days of alerts and tickets and sort them by type. Choose the type that comes up most often and follows the same steps every time. That becomes the first playbook, and the others wait until it works.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Brief the playbook the way you would brief a new analyst. Say what sets it off and who decides at each step. Emergent builds the automation from those sentences. Spell out every point where a person has to choose before anything changes.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Define what separates a Sev 1 from a Sev 2, and who gets paged at each level. Set how long a page can go unacknowledged before it escalates, and name a secondary for every rotation to cover nights and holidays.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Connect your monitoring service and identity provider through their APIs, along with the email security tool. Each alert should carry the fields the playbook reads, such as the host and the user. Add your chat tool so incident channels and approvals sit where responders work.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Decide what waits for a person
fields.howto_step_5_des: Mark which steps run unattended and which wait for approval. Lookups and grouping can run on their own. Disabling an account or isolating a laptop should wait for an analyst's click, with the evidence shown beside the button.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Feed last quarter's alerts through the automation before it touches live systems. Check that every one grouped correctly, reached the right person, and stopped at the approval step. Adjust the playbook by prompting wherever one went wrong, and replay until the set comes back clean.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Go live with the playbook you tested most and watch a month of real incidents. Compare time to acknowledge and time to mitigate with the numbers from your replay, then switch on the next one.

This page shows four playbooks a lean security or IT team actually runs, drawn as working screens: a phishing burst grouped into one incident and purged on an analyst approval, a suspicious sign-in held for one click before sessions are revoked, an outage page that escalates when nobody acknowledges, and a review timeline built from the incident record. The lifecycle (NIST), SOAR versus automation, and metrics are answered in the FAQ.

claims_to_source: NIST SP 800-61 Revision 2 described four incident response phases: preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication, and recovery; and post-incident activity
NIST SP 800-61 Revision 3, published April 2025, superseded Revision 2 and ties incident response to the Cybersecurity Framework 2.0
Security orchestration connects tools and passes data between them, while security automation runs repeatable steps that replace manual work; SOAR platforms combine them
An escalation policy notifies one level at a time and moves to the next level when no one acknowledges before the escalation timeout
Mean time to acknowledge measures how long a team takes to acknowledge an incident; mean time to resolve measures how long it takes to fully resolve it
A blameless postmortem records the impact, timeline, contributing causes, and follow-up action items without blaming a person
Identity providers flag atypical travel: sign-ins from distant locations in a time frame that makes real travel unlikely
